title: Tenses
notes: Tense is a verb form that shows the time of an action or state — past, present, or future. English has three main tenses: Present, Past, and Future. Each main tense has four aspects: Simple, Continuous (Progressive), Perfect, and Perfect Continuous. This gives English a total of twelve tense forms. Tense is one of the most important grammar topics in the NEB Class 11 English syllabus and appears frequently in both objective and descriptive questions.

The present simple tense is used for: (1) habits and routines — 'I wake up at six every day.' (2) General truths and facts — 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.' (3) Permanent situations — 'She lives in Pokhara.' (4) Scheduled events — 'The train leaves at 9 AM.' The form is: subject + base verb (add -s/-es for third person singular). Negative: do not/does not + base verb. Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb? Time markers: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day/week/year.

The present continuous tense describes actions happening right now or around the present time. Form: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. Uses: (1) Actions happening at the moment of speaking — 'She is writing a letter.' (2) Temporary situations — 'I am staying with my cousin this week.' (3) Future arrangements — 'We are meeting them tomorrow.' (4) Changing situations — 'The climate is getting warmer.' Important: Stative verbs (know, believe, belong, love, hate, seem, understand) are generally NOT used in continuous forms. We say 'I know him', not 'I am knowing him'.

The present perfect tense connects the past with the present. Form: subject + has/have + past participle. Uses: (1) Actions completed at an unspecified time — 'I have visited Chitwan.' (2) Actions that started in the past and continue to the present — 'She has lived here for ten years.' (3) Recent actions with present results — 'I have lost my keys' (so I can't enter now). (4) Life experiences — 'He has read all of Shakespeare.' Time markers: already, yet, just, ever, never, recently, so far, up to now, since, for.

The present perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action that started in the past and continues to the present, or has just finished with visible results. Form: subject + has/have + been + verb-ing. Example: 'I have been studying English since 2019.' Compare with present perfect: 'I have studied English for five years' (focus on completion/amount) vs. 'I have been studying English for five years' (focus on the ongoing activity). Both are grammatically correct but carry slightly different emphasis.

The past simple tense describes completed actions at a specific time in the past. Form: subject + past form of verb (regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs have unique past forms). Uses: (1) Completed actions — 'I went to Kathmandu last year.' (2) Series of completed actions — 'He woke up, had breakfast, and left for school.' (3) Past habits — 'I played cricket every evening when I was young.' Time markers: yesterday, last week/year, ago, in 2010, when I was a child. Regular past form: add -ed (walked, played). Irregular past forms must be memorised (go→went, see→saw, eat→ate).

The past continuous tense describes actions that were in progress at a specific time in the past. Form: subject + was/were + verb-ing. Uses: (1) An action in progress at a specific past time — 'At 8 PM yesterday, I was watching TV.' (2) A longer action interrupted by a shorter one — 'I was sleeping when the phone rang.' (The continuous tense for the longer action; simple past for the interruption.) (3) Two simultaneous ongoing actions — 'While I was cooking, she was cleaning.' Time markers: while, when, as, at 5 PM yesterday, all day yesterday.

The past perfect tense describes an action completed before another action or time in the past. It is the 'past before the past.' Form: subject + had + past participle. Example: 'When I reached the station, the train had already left.' The leaving happened before the reaching. Use 'had + past participle' for the earlier action and simple past for the later action. Time markers: already, just, never, before, by the time, until then. This tense is essential for narrative writing and is frequently tested in gap-filling exercises.

The past perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action that was ongoing before another past action or time. Form: subject + had + been + verb-ing. Example: 'She had been waiting for two hours when the bus finally arrived.' This highlights that the waiting started before the bus arrived and continued up to that point. Compare: 'She had waited for two hours' (focus on completion) vs. 'She had been waiting for two hours' (focus on the prolonged activity). Use this tense when the duration is important to the meaning.

The future simple tense describes actions that will happen after the present moment. Form: subject + will/shall + base verb. Uses: (1) Predictions — 'It will rain tomorrow.' (2) Spontaneous decisions — 'I will help you with your homework.' (3) Promises and offers — 'I will never forget this.' (4) Future facts — 'The sun will rise at 6 AM.' Note: 'Shall' is used with I and we in formal British English for future (I shall, we shall), though 'will' is acceptable everywhere. In American English, 'will' is used with all persons.

The future continuous tense describes actions that will be in progress at a specific time in the future. Form: subject + will be + verb-ing. Example: 'This time tomorrow, I will be travelling to Pokhara.' It can also describe parallel actions in the future: 'While you will be sleeping, I will be studying.' This tense can also be used for polite enquiries about someone's plans: 'Will you be using the car tonight?'

The future perfect tense describes an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future. Form: subject + will have + past participle. Example: 'By next year, I will have graduated from school.' The graduation will be completed before next year arrives. Time markers: by the time, by next year/month/day, before, when. This tense is commonly tested in gap-filling exercises where the time marker 'by + future time' signals its use.

The future perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action up to a point in the future. Form: subject + will have been + verb-ing. Example: 'By December, I will have been studying English for five years.' This combines the future perfect (completion by a future point) with the continuous aspect (duration). Use this tense when you want to stress how long an action will have been going on by a particular future moment.

Present: Simple (I write), Continuous (I am writing), Perfect (I have written), Perfect Continuous (I have been writing). Past: Simple (I wrote), Continuous (I was writing), Perfect (I had written), Perfect Continuous (I had been writing). Future: Simple (I will write), Continuous (I will be writing), Perfect (I will have written), Perfect Continuous (I will have been writing). The key to mastering tenses is understanding aspect: simple (completed/habitual), continuous (ongoing/in progress), perfect (completed before a reference point), perfect continuous (duration up to a reference point).

Stative verbs (also called state verbs) describe states rather than actions and are generally NOT used in continuous tenses. Categories include: Thought (know, believe, understand, remember, forget, suppose, mean). Emotion (love, like, hate, prefer, want, need, hope, wish). Sense/perception (see, hear, smell, taste, feel, recognize). Possession (have, possess, belong, own). Being/state (be, seem, appear, cost, weigh). Exception: Some stative verbs can be used in continuous form when they have a different meaning. 'I am having lunch' (eating = action) vs. 'I have a car' (possession = state). 'The soup tastes good' (perception) vs. 'She is tasting the soup' (action of sampling).

When reporting speech, tense shifting (backshifting) usually occurs: Present simple → past simple ('I like apples' → She said she liked apples). Present continuous → past continuous. Present perfect → past perfect. Past simple → past perfect. Future (will) → conditional (would). However, backshifting is NOT done when: (1) The reported information is still true — 'The Earth revolves around the Sun' (reported as present simple). (2) The reporting verb is in present/future tense — 'He says he is tired.' (3) Using modal verbs that have no past form (ought to, might, could, would, should).

Each tense has characteristic time markers that signal its use. Present simple: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day, on Mondays. Present continuous: now, at the moment, currently, today, this week. Present perfect: already, yet, just, ever, never, recently, so far, since, for. Past simple: yesterday, last week, ago, in 1999, when I was young. Past perfect: already, just, never, before, by the time. Future simple: tomorrow, next week, in 2030, soon. Recognising these markers quickly helps in gap-filling and tense conversion exercises in NEB exams.
confusion: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple: Use past simple with a specific past time (I saw him yesterday). Use present perfect without a specific past time or with 'since/for' (I have seen him / I have known him for years). You CANNOT use present perfect with words like 'yesterday', 'last week', 'ago', 'in 1990'.

Past Simple vs. Past Perfect: Past perfect is used for the earlier of two past actions. 'When I arrived, the movie started' means they happened simultaneously. 'When I arrived, the movie had started' means the movie began before I arrived. Always use past perfect for the action that happened first when two past actions are described together.

Will vs. Shall: Traditionally, 'shall' is used with I and we for simple future (I shall go, we shall see). 'Will' is used with all persons. In modern English, 'will' is used with all persons in both British and American English. 'Shall' survives mainly in questions with I/we (Shall we dance? Shall I open the window?) and in formal/legal language.

Present Perfect Continuous vs. Present Perfect: Use present perfect simple for completed actions with present results (I have painted the room — it's done). Use present perfect continuous for ongoing actions emphasising duration (I have been painting the room — I may still be working on it). Some verbs (know, believe, have) are rarely used in continuous forms even for duration.

Past Simple vs. Past Continuous: Past simple describes completed actions (I read the book). Past continuous describes ongoing actions at a specific past time (I was reading when you called). When both appear in one sentence, the continuous form is the background action and the simple form is the interrupting action.

Will vs. Going to: 'Going to' is used for planned intentions and predictions with present evidence (Look at those clouds! It's going to rain). 'Will' is used for spontaneous decisions, predictions without evidence, promises, and offers (I will help you). In NEB exams, distinguishing these is tested through gap-filling and sentence transformation.

Since vs. For with Perfect Tenses: 'Since' marks the starting point of an action (since 2015, since Monday, since I was a child). 'For' marks the duration (for five years, for two hours, for a long time). Both are used with perfect tenses, but never interchangeably: 'I have lived here since 2015' vs. 'I have lived here for nine years'.
practice: Fill in the correct tense: She ___ (write) a letter right now. [Answer: is writing]
Fill in the correct tense: They ___ (know) each other since childhood. [Answer: have known]
Fill in the correct tense: By the time we reached the station, the train ___ (leave). [Answer: had already left]
Fill in the correct tense: I ___ (wait) for two hours when the bus finally arrived. [Answer: had been waiting]
Change to reported speech: 'I am reading a novel,' said Ram. [Answer: Ram said that he was reading a novel.]
Change to reported speech: 'I will help you tomorrow,' said Sita. [Answer: Sita said that she would help me the next day.]
Correct the error: I have seen him yesterday. [Answer: I saw him yesterday.]
Correct the error: She has worked here since three years. [Answer: She has worked here for three years.]
Fill in the correct form: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we will stay indoors. [Answer: rains — first conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb]
Fill in the correct form: I wish I ___ (be) taller. [Answer: were — second conditional/wish for present unreal]
universalFacts: English is unusual among European languages in having a rich tense-aspect system. Many languages (like Chinese and Japanese) do not have grammatical tense at all, expressing time through context and time words instead.

The English present perfect tense has no direct equivalent in many languages, making it one of the most difficult concepts for Nepali-speaking learners, since Nepali uses a single past tense (या/यो) that covers both simple past and present perfect meanings.

The distinction between simple and continuous aspects is present in nearly all Indo-European languages but is expressed differently. In English, the continuous aspect uses the auxiliary 'be' + '-ing', a pattern inherited from Old English.

In the NEB English examination, tense questions typically appear in gap-filling (3-5 marks), error correction (2-3 marks), and sentence transformation (2-3 marks), making this topic one of the highest-yield grammar areas for exam preparation.

The use of 'shall' with first person is increasingly rare in modern English, especially in American English. Most native speakers now use 'will' with all persons. However, NEB exams may still test traditional usage, so students should know both forms.

Stative verbs are a uniquely English challenge because many verbs that are stative in English can be used dynamically in other languages. For example, 'I am thinking about the answer' (process) vs. 'I think the answer is correct' (opinion/state).
